methods.label: Turn the equation into a product
methods.explanation:
Because \(m\) and \(n\) must be integers, it helps to turn the equation into a product with very few integer factor pairs. Rearranging and adding \(1\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
m+n=mn
&\iff mn-m-n+1=1\\
&\iff (m-1)(n-1)=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Two integers have product \(1\) only when both are \(1\) or both are \(-1\). Thus
\[
(m-1,n-1)=(1,1)\quad\text{or}\quad(-1,-1),
\]
which gives
\[
(m,n)=(2,2)\quad\text{or}\quad(0,0).
\]
Both pairs satisfy the original equation. Every solution must come from one of these two factor pairs, and each factor pair determines exactly one ordered pair \((m,n)\). Therefore there are exactly \(2\) pairs, choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
methods.levelReason: The proof uses a quadratic product identity and the elementary integer factor pairs of 1, without formal number-theory machinery.
